question: What is the relative charge of a proton?
Which particle has no electrical charge?
What is the approximate diameter of an atom?
In the nuclear model of the atom, where is almost all the mass concentrated?
Which type of radiation is deflected by a magnetic field but has the least penetrating power?
What is emitted during gamma decay?
An alpha particle consists of which particles?
A radioactive sample has a half-life of 10 years. After 30 years, what fraction of the original activity remains?
What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
options: The time for all atoms to decay
The time for half the atoms to decay
The time for activity to double
The time for the nucleus to split
correct: The time for half the atoms to decay

question: Beta decay occurs when a neutron changes into a proton and emits which particle?
What is nuclear fission?
options: A large nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei
An electron being emitted from a nucleus
A gamma ray being absorbed by a nucleus
correct: A large nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei

question: Which fuel is used in nuclear fusion reactions in stars?
Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but different numbers of which particle?
Which type of radiation has the greatest penetrating power?
In a nuclear chain reaction, what triggers further fission events?
The number of protons in an atom is called the __________ number.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus is called the __________ number.
Alpha radiation can be stopped by a few centimetres of __________.
Beta radiation can be stopped by a few millimetres of __________.
Gamma radiation can be reduced by several centimetres of __________.
The activity of a radioactive source is measured in __________.
A nuclear chain reaction must be controlled in a nuclear __________ to produce electricity safely.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called __________.
Nuclear fusion releases energy because the products have less __________ than the reactants.
Radioactive decay is a __________ process, meaning it cannot be predicted for a single atom.
Match each type of radiation to its description.
Match each type of radiation to what it is stopped by.

pairs.definition: A few centimetres of air or paper
Several centimetres of lead or thick concrete

question: Match each subatomic particle to its relative charge.
Match each nuclear process to its correct description.

pairs.definition: A large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei
Two small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus
An unstable nucleus emits radiation spontaneously

question: Match each term to its correct meaning.

pairs.definition: Time for half the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay
Number of nuclear decays per second

question: State what is meant by the term 'isotope'.
mark_scheme: Atoms of the same element (1) with different numbers of neutrons (1).

question: Describe the structure of an atom, including the location and charge of each subatomic particle.
mark_scheme: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus (1); protons have +1 charge, neutrons have 0 charge (1); electrons orbit the nucleus in shells and have -1 charge (1). [max 2]

question: Explain why alpha radiation is the most ionising but least penetrating type of nuclear radiation.
mark_scheme: Alpha particles are large/have +2 charge so interact strongly with matter and cause ionisation easily (1); this means they lose energy quickly and cannot travel far / are absorbed quickly (1).

question: Describe what happens to the nucleus of an atom when it emits a beta particle.
mark_scheme: A neutron changes into a proton (1); a beta particle (fast-moving electron) is emitted from the nucleus (1).

question: Explain why the count rate of a radioactive source decreases over time.
mark_scheme: Radioactive decay is a random process (1); over time, the number of unstable nuclei in the sample decreases (1); fewer unstable nuclei means fewer decays per second, so activity/count rate falls (1).

question: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 5 years. If the initial activity is 800 Bq, calculate the activity after 15 years.
mark_scheme: Number of half-lives = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 (1); activity = 800 ÷ 2³ = 800 ÷ 8 = 100 Bq (1).

question: State two products of a nuclear fission reaction.
mark_scheme: Any two from: two smaller (daughter) nuclei (1); neutrons (1); energy / gamma radiation (1).

question: Describe how a chain reaction occurs in nuclear fission.
mark_scheme: A neutron is absorbed by a uranium nucleus causing it to split (1); fission releases further neutrons (1); these neutrons go on to split more nuclei, sustaining the reaction (1).

question: State one similarity and one difference between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
mark_scheme: Similarity: both release large amounts of energy / both are nuclear reactions (1); difference: fission splits a large nucleus / fusion joins small nuclei (1).

question: Explain why Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment led to the nuclear model replacing the plum pudding model.
mark_scheme: Most alpha particles passed straight through (suggesting the atom is mostly empty space) (1); some were deflected at large angles, suggesting a small, dense, positively charged nucleus exists (1).

question: Explain why workers in nuclear power stations must wear film badges and follow strict safety procedures.
mark_scheme: Ionising radiation can damage living cells / DNA (1); this can cause mutations leading to cancer (1); film badges monitor exposure levels to ensure dose remains below safe limits / protective clothing limits exposure (1).

question: Describe what happens to the mass number and atomic number of a nucleus when it emits an alpha particle.
mark_scheme: Mass number decreases by 4 (1); atomic number decreases by 2 (1).

question: Explain how our understanding of atomic structure changed from the plum pudding model to the nuclear model, and describe the evidence that led to this change.
mark_scheme: Plum pudding model: atom as a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it (1); Geiger-Marsden alpha scattering experiment: alpha particles fired at gold foil (1); most passed straight through — atom is mostly empty space (1); some deflected at large angles — small, dense, positively charged nucleus exists (1). Accept any 4 creditworthy points.

question: Compare the properties of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation in terms of their nature, charge, penetrating power, and ionising ability.
mark_scheme: Alpha: helium nucleus, +2 charge, stopped by paper/few cm air, highly ionising (1); Beta: fast electron, -1 charge, stopped by aluminium, moderately ionising (1); Gamma: EM radiation, no charge, reduced by lead/thick concrete, weakly ionising (1); clear comparison of at least two properties across all three types (1).

question: Evaluate the use of radioactive isotopes in medicine, including the benefits and risks. Refer to the importance of half-life in choosing a suitable isotope.
mark_scheme: Uses: diagnosis using tracers (e.g. technetium-99m) / cancer treatment using radiotherapy (1); benefit: can target tumours / diagnose conditions non-invasively (1); risk: radiation can damage healthy cells / cause cancer (1); short half-life preferred for tracers — reduces patient radiation dose (1); isotope must remain active long enough for procedure to be completed (1).

question: Explain how a nuclear power station uses fission to generate electricity, and discuss one advantage and one disadvantage of nuclear power compared to burning fossil fuels.
mark_scheme: Uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission, releasing energy (1); energy heats water to produce steam (1); steam drives a turbine connected to a generator (1); advantage: no carbon dioxide / greenhouse gas emissions during operation (1); disadvantage: produces radioactive waste that is difficult and expensive to dispose of safely (1).

question: Evaluate nuclear fusion as a future energy source. In your answer, explain the process of fusion, why it is difficult to achieve on Earth, and whether you think it is a viable solution to the world's energy needs.
mark_scheme: Fusion: two light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen isotopes) join to form a heavier nucleus (1); releases large amounts of energy because products have less mass than reactants (1); requires extremely high temperatures and pressures to overcome electrostatic repulsion between nuclei (1); difficult to contain plasma at these temperatures — no material can withstand it, requiring magnetic confinement (e.g. tokamak) (1); advantages: fuel (hydrogen) is abundant / no long-lived radioactive waste / no greenhouse gases (1); disadvantage: not yet achieved commercially / energy input currently exceeds output / very expensive research (1). Award marks for well-reasoned conclusion supported by evidence.

question: A hospital is choosing a radioactive isotope to use as a medical tracer. Evaluate the factors that must be considered, including type of radiation emitted, half-life, and how it will be used safely.
mark_scheme: Must emit gamma radiation so it can be detected outside the body (1); alpha and beta would be absorbed by tissue and cause damage (1); half-life should be short enough to minimise patient radiation dose (1); but long enough that the tracer remains active for the duration of the scan (1); patient and staff must be protected — staff use shielding, limit exposure time, monitor doses with film badges (1); isotope should be chemically suitable to be taken up by target organ/tissue (1).

question: Explain how scientists use carbon-14 to date archaeological samples, and state one limitation of this method.
mark_scheme: Carbon-14 is absorbed by living organisms during their lifetime in a known ratio to carbon-12 (1); when the organism dies, no more carbon-14 is absorbed and it begins to decay (1); by measuring the ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 remaining, scientists can calculate how long ago the organism died using the known half-life of carbon-14 (5730 years) (1); limitation: only useful for organic materials / only reliable up to around 50,000 years (1).

question: Describe the structure of an atom in terms of the subatomic particles it contains. Include their location, relative mass and relative charge.
mark_scheme: Protons: in nucleus, relative mass 1, charge +1 (1); neutrons: in nucleus, relative mass 1, charge 0 (1); electrons: orbit nucleus in shells, relative mass negligible (~1/2000), charge −1 (1); nucleus is tiny compared to the atom — most of atom is empty space (1).

question: Explain what isotopes are and give an example. Explain why isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties but different physical properties.
mark_scheme: Isotopes: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons (1); example: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 (or other valid pair) (1); same chemical properties because same number of electrons — same electron configuration determines chemistry (1); different physical properties (e.g. density, radioactivity) because they have different mass numbers (1).

question: A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 6400 Bq and a half-life of 8 days. Calculate the activity after 40 days. Show your working clearly.
mark_scheme: Number of half-lives = 40/8 = 5 (1); after each half-life activity halves: 6400 → 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 → 200 Bq (1); activity after 40 days = 200 Bq (1); clear working shown (1).

question: Explain why alpha radiation is dangerous inside the body but relatively safe outside the body. Contrast this with gamma radiation.
mark_scheme: Alpha particles are highly ionising — cause significant damage to cells/DNA (1); stopped by a few cm of air or skin — cannot penetrate into body from outside (1); if inhaled or ingested, alpha source is directly next to internal cells — highly dangerous (1); gamma: weakly ionising but highly penetrating — can pass through body from outside causing damage to internal organs (1).

question: Describe the Thomson plum pudding model of the atom and explain what evidence led to it being replaced by the nuclear model.
mark_scheme: Thomson model: atom as a uniform sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded within it (1); Geiger-Marsden experiment: alpha particles fired at thin gold foil (1); most passed straight through — mostly empty space (1); some deflected at large angles / bounced back — small, dense, positive nucleus at centre (1).

question: Explain what is meant by background radiation. Give three sources of background radiation and explain why it must be accounted for in experiments.
mark_scheme: Background radiation is low-level ionising radiation present in the environment at all times (1); sources: cosmic rays, radon gas from rocks/soil, medical X-rays, food/drink, nuclear power (1) (1) — two sources for 2 marks; must subtract from readings as it contributes to count rate — would give artificially high results (1).

question: A sample contains 80 g of a radioactive isotope. After 60 years only 10 g remains undecayed. Calculate the half-life of the isotope.
mark_scheme: Fraction remaining = 10/80 = 1/8 (1); 1/8 = (1/2)³ so 3 half-lives have passed (1); half-life = 60/3 = 20 years (1); clear working shown (1).

question: Explain the role of control rods and moderator in a nuclear reactor. Explain what would happen if the control rods were fully removed.
mark_scheme: Moderator (e.g. water or graphite): slows down neutrons so they are more easily absorbed by uranium fuel (1); control rods (e.g. boron): absorb neutrons to control rate of fission (1); lowering control rods absorbs more neutrons slowing reaction (1); if fully removed: more neutrons available, more fission events, chain reaction grows uncontrolled — potential meltdown (1).

question: Describe how alpha, beta and gamma radiation behave in a magnetic field. Explain what this tells us about their nature.
mark_scheme: Alpha (+2 charge): deflected in one direction by magnetic field (1); beta (−1 charge): deflected in opposite direction, to greater extent due to smaller mass (1); gamma (no charge): not deflected (1); deflection confirms alpha and beta are charged particles; lack of deflection confirms gamma is electromagnetic radiation with no charge (1).

question: Explain why nuclear fusion releases energy. Why does it require extremely high temperatures to initiate the reaction?
mark_scheme: In fusion, two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus (1); the product has less mass than the sum of the reactants — mass converted to energy (E = mc²) (1); extremely high temperatures needed because nuclei are both positively charged (1); must have enough kinetic energy to overcome electrostatic repulsion and get close enough for strong nuclear force to bind them (1).

question: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. A wooden artefact contains 25% of the carbon-14 that a living tree would contain. Calculate the age of the artefact.
mark_scheme: 25% = 1/4 of original (1); 1/4 = (1/2)² so 2 half-lives have passed (1); age = 2 × 5730 = 11 460 years (1); clear working shown (1).

question: Explain how the Bohr model of the atom improved on Rutherford's nuclear model. What evidence supported Bohr's model?
mark_scheme: Rutherford's model had electrons orbiting nucleus but could not explain why they did not spiral into nucleus (1); Bohr proposed electrons occupy fixed energy levels/shells (1); electrons can only gain or lose specific amounts of energy to move between levels (1); emission spectra — atoms emit specific wavelengths of light when electrons fall to lower energy levels — matches Bohr's predicted energy levels (1).

question: Explain the processes of alpha decay and beta decay. For each, describe what changes occur to the nucleus in terms of proton number and mass number. Give a nuclear equation for each.
mark_scheme: Alpha decay: nucleus emits a helium nucleus (2p + 2n) (1); mass number decreases by 4, proton number decreases by 2 (1); e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He (1); beta decay: neutron changes to proton and emits electron (beta particle) (1); mass number unchanged, proton number increases by 1 (1).

question: Evaluate the use of nuclear power stations to generate electricity, considering safety, environmental impact, reliability and the problem of nuclear waste.
mark_scheme: Reliability: generates electricity continuously regardless of weather — unlike renewables (1); environmental: no CO₂ emissions during operation — helps reduce climate change (1); produces highly radioactive waste that remains dangerous for thousands of years (1); risk of accidents — Chernobyl, Fukushima — public safety concern (1); high cost to build, run and decommission (1).

question: Explain why half-life is the most appropriate measure of how quickly a radioactive source decays, rather than measuring the time for all atoms to decay. Include how half-life is determined from a decay graph.
mark_scheme: Radioactive decay is random — cannot predict when any specific atom will decay (1); total time to fully decay is theoretically infinite (1); half-life is constant for a given isotope — unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state (1); from a graph: read activity at t=0, find time for activity to halve — repeat from different starting points and average (1); constant half-life confirms exponential decay pattern (1).

question: Describe the key experiments that led to our modern understanding of the atom from Dalton's model to the nuclear model. Include the contribution of Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr.
mark_scheme: Dalton: solid indivisible spheres (1); Thomson: discovered electron — plum pudding model with electrons embedded in positive sphere (1); Rutherford (Geiger-Marsden): alpha scattering experiment showed mostly empty space with small dense positive nucleus (1); Rutherford's nuclear model with electrons orbiting nucleus (1); Bohr: electrons occupy fixed energy levels — explains atomic emission spectra (1).

question: Evaluate the use of ionising radiation in cancer treatment. Include the type of radiation used, how it works, the benefits and the risks to the patient.
mark_scheme: Gamma radiation used in radiotherapy (1); high-energy gamma rays damage DNA of cancer cells preventing reproduction (1); beams focused on tumour from multiple angles to maximise dose to tumour and minimise dose to healthy tissue (1); benefit: can destroy tumours non-surgically (1); risk: radiation can damage healthy cells and cause secondary cancers (1).

question: Explain how a nuclear chain reaction is initiated and controlled in a nuclear power station. Describe what is meant by critical mass.
mark_scheme: Neutron absorbed by ²³⁵U nucleus causing it to become unstable and split (1); fission releases 2–3 more neutrons (1); these cause further fission — chain reaction (1); critical mass: minimum amount of fissile material needed to sustain chain reaction (1); below critical mass, too many neutrons escape without causing fission — reaction dies (1).

question: The activity of a radioactive source is measured every 10 minutes. Results: 0 min = 1200 Bq; 10 min = 600 Bq; 20 min = 300 Bq; 30 min = 150 Bq. Determine the half-life, then calculate what the activity would be after 1 hour.
mark_scheme: Activity halves every 10 minutes — half-life = 10 minutes (1); confirmed by consistent halving in all intervals (1); after 60 minutes: 6 half-lives have passed (1); 1200 ÷ 2⁶ = 1200 ÷ 64 = 18.75 Bq (1); correct calculation shown (1).

question: Explain why radioactive decay is described as a random and spontaneous process. Explain what this means for the behaviour of a single atom compared to a large sample.
mark_scheme: Random: impossible to predict exactly when any individual atom will decay (1); each atom has the same probability of decaying in any given time period (1); spontaneous: decay is not triggered by external conditions — temperature, pressure, chemical state have no effect (1); for a single atom: can only state a probability of decay — not certain when (1); for large sample: statistical behaviour is predictable — constant half-life observed (1).

question: Describe the nuclear reactions that power stars such as the Sun. Explain why stars eventually die and what happens to them after they run out of fuel.
mark_scheme: Sun fuses hydrogen nuclei (protons) to form helium nuclei (1); releases enormous amounts of energy as electromagnetic radiation (1); this requires temperatures of ~15 million K at the core (1); when hydrogen fuel runs out, star expands into a red giant (1); core collapses — smaller stars become white dwarfs; larger stars may become neutron stars or black holes (1).

question: Evaluate the evidence for the nuclear model of the atom from the Geiger-Marsden experiment. Describe the results and explain how each observation supported the nuclear model.
mark_scheme: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil (1); most passed straight through: atom is mostly empty space (1); a small number were deflected at large angles: indicates a small, concentrated region of positive charge (nucleus) (1); a very few bounced almost straight back: nucleus is very dense and massive (1); this disproved the plum pudding model — positive charge not spread throughout (1).

question: Evaluate the risks and benefits of using radioactive materials in medicine. Consider diagnosis (tracers), treatment (radiotherapy) and sterilisation of medical equipment. Include precautions taken to protect patients and staff.
mark_scheme: Tracers: gamma emitters injected and detected outside body — non-invasive diagnosis (1); short half-life minimises patient dose (1); radiotherapy: gamma/beta radiation destroys cancer cells (1); risk: can damage healthy tissue causing side effects (1); sterilisation: gamma radiation kills bacteria on surgical instruments without heating (1); staff protection: lead shielding, film badges to monitor exposure, minimise time near sources, distance from sources (1).

question: Explain in detail how a nuclear power station generates electricity. Include the fission reaction, how energy is transferred to the turbines, the role of the cooling system and how waste heat is managed.
mark_scheme: ²³⁵U absorbs neutron, becomes unstable and splits into two smaller nuclei and 2–3 neutrons (1); releases large amounts of kinetic energy / heat (1); heat used to boil water — steam produced (1); steam drives turbines connected to generators producing electricity (1); coolant (water) circulates to carry heat from reactor to steam generator (1); waste heat (not converted to electricity) released via cooling towers as water vapour (1).

question: Evaluate the use of radioisotopes with different half-lives for different medical and industrial applications. Explain why choosing the correct half-life is critical, using at least three specific examples.
mark_scheme: Medical tracer (e.g. technetium-99m, half-life 6 hours): short enough to limit patient dose but long enough for scan to complete (1); carbon-14 (half-life 5730 years): useful for archaeological dating up to ~50 000 years (1); iodine-131 (half-life 8 days): used to treat thyroid cancer — taken up by thyroid, beta/gamma destroys cancer cells (1); industrial thickness gauging: medium half-life needed so source stays useful for months without replacement (1); smoke detectors: americium-241 (half-life 432 years) chosen so detector works for decades (1); too short a half-life means source becomes useless quickly; too long means unnecessary prolonged exposure (1).

question: Explain the development of the model of the atom from ancient Greece to the modern nuclear model. Describe the evidence that led to each change in the model.
mark_scheme: Ancient Greeks: indivisible solid atoms — no experimental evidence (1); Dalton (1803): solid spheres — based on chemical combining ratios (1); Thomson (1897): discovered electrons — proposed plum pudding model (1); Rutherford (1911): Geiger-Marsden alpha scattering showed nuclear model — small dense positive nucleus (1); Bohr (1913): electrons in fixed energy levels — explained emission spectra (1); modern model: quantum mechanical model with electron clouds / probability distributions (1).

question: Evaluate nuclear fusion as a potential energy source for the future. In your answer, compare it with nuclear fission, consider the technical challenges and assess how close we are to commercial fusion power.
mark_scheme: Fusion: joins light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) releasing energy; fission: splits heavy nuclei (uranium) (1); fusion fuel (deuterium/tritium) more abundant than uranium (1); fusion produces no long-lived radioactive waste — significant advantage over fission (1); technical challenge: requires ~100 million K to overcome electrostatic repulsion (1); plasma must be contained — no material can withstand this temperature, so magnetic confinement (tokamak/ITER) used (1); currently energy input exceeds output — not yet commercially viable (1).

question: Explain fully how nuclear radiation can cause harm to living organisms. Include the mechanisms of ionisation, the effects on DNA and cells, and distinguish between the risks from different types of radiation.
mark_scheme: Ionising radiation removes electrons from atoms in cells creating ions (1); ions can disrupt chemical reactions in cells (1); radiation can break or alter DNA strands (1); damaged DNA can lead to mutations — uncontrolled cell division = cancer (1); high doses can kill cells directly — radiation sickness (1); alpha: most ionising but only internal hazard — stopped by skin (1); beta: penetrates skin but not deep tissue (1); gamma: penetrates whole body — causes damage throughout (1) — any six.

question: Evaluate the long-term storage and disposal of high-level nuclear waste from power stations. Consider the scientific, environmental and social challenges involved.
mark_scheme: High-level waste remains dangerously radioactive for thousands of years (1); must be isolated from the environment — cannot be allowed to enter water supply or food chain (1); currently stored in cooling ponds then vitrified (encased in glass) (1); deep geological repositories (underground storage in stable rock) proposed as permanent solution (1); challenge: must remain safe for >10 000 years — longer than any human civilisation has existed (1); public opposition — communities unwilling to host sites (1); cost enormous and ultimately paid by taxpayers (1) — any six.

question: Explain in detail how the chain reaction in a nuclear weapon differs from that in a nuclear reactor, and explain how reactor design prevents a nuclear explosion.
mark_scheme: Reactor: controlled chain reaction — each fission triggers on average exactly one further fission (critical) (1); control rods absorb excess neutrons to regulate reaction rate (1); coolant removes heat at controlled rate — used to generate steam/electricity (1); if control rods fully inserted, reaction stops — inherently controllable (1); weapon: supercritical chain reaction — each fission triggers more than one further fission (1); uncontrolled exponential growth of fissions in microseconds releases enormous energy as explosion (1); reactor cannot explode like a bomb because fuel is not in the correct configuration or concentration for supercritical mass (1) — any six.
